1.Nf3 d5 2.g3.name: King's Indian Attack
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3.background: Its grandmaster use began as an offshoot of the widespread King's Indian Defence of the 1950s. Prominent players of it include Bobby Fischer (mostly early in his career), Mikhail Botvinnik, Vasily Smyslov and Tigran Petrosian; today it is relatively uncommon at grandmaster level but popular at club level.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and controls e4, where White would like to put a pawn. Black commits to nothing: a solid pawn centre, an early bishop sortie or a mirrored fianchetto all stay possible. The cost is that White's slow set-up is not yet challenged.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5.name: King's Indian Attack: Sicilian Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5.strategy: Claims queenside space and eyes d4, aiming for a King's Indian set-up with the colours reversed. Black fights for the centre at once, but no pawn backs d5, so White can strike with c4 against it or d4 against c5. The game turns on whether Black's centre holds.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and keeps the c8-bishop free to leave the pawn chain before …e6 would shut it in. The pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight, which therefore develops via d7. Black gets a sturdy but slightly passive centre against White's slow build-up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4.name: King's Indian Attack: Keres Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the c8-bishop outside the pawn chain before …e6 can lock it in. It has little to bite on, though: the f3-knight is backed by the e2-pawn, and h3 or Ne5 soon asks the bishop to decide whether to take the knight and give White the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once and prepares …e5. The knight blocks the c-pawn, though, so d5 has no support from …c6 and White can pressure it with c4 or take space with d4. Sound enough, but it commits the knight before the structure is clear.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before …e6, so it is not shut in behind its own pawns. Played this early it allows 3.Nh4, which hits the bishop; after …Bg6 Nxg6 hxg6 Black has doubled g-pawns and has given up the bishop pair. Playable, but it gives White something to aim at.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and frees the f8-bishop, but shuts the c8-bishop in before it has left. White builds slowly with the fianchetto, castling and a later e4, and the c8-bishop has to find a role on b7 or d7. Sound, but passive.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6.name: King's Indian Attack: Double Fianchetto
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors the fianchetto, so both king's bishops aim down the long diagonals. The d5-pawn is guarded only by the queen for now, and the bishop on g7 does not help it, so c4 tests it at once. Sound, but more committal than …Nf6.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 b6.strategy: Sound but slow: it prepares ...Bb7, though with the pawn on d5 that bishop would look only at its own pawn, and it loosens c6 and the long diagonal towards a8. White develops freely and can challenge d5 with c4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space without developing a piece and loosens c6 and the long diagonal towards a8. Playable, but the pawn can become a target for a4 or c4 while White simply develops.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that has no role yet, at best preparing ...b5. The cost is small against White's slow set-up, so it is playable, but White is free to develop and then claim the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 a5.strategy: A rim pawn move: it stops b4 and gains space for ...a4, but develops nothing. The cost is small, so it is playable, but White can ignore it and develop at leisure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 h6.strategy: A slow move that takes g5 from White's knight and bishop but develops nothing. The cost is small, so it is playable; White uses the tempo to develop and prepare a central break.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 h5.strategy: Gains space on the flank but spends a tempo without developing a piece. The pawn cannot go on to h4, since Nxh4 wins it with g3 guarding the knight. Playable, but it does little for Black's game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 f6.strategy: Prepares …e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. White takes the centre while Black's development lags.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 f5.strategy: Aims for a Dutch-style set-up, but the pawn weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal and leaves e5 as an outpost for White's knight. Black must still develop every piece behind it, while White castles and builds.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 d4.strategy: Gains space before any piece is out, but the pawn becomes a target for c3 or e3 and the f3-knight. Black has to hold it, while White castles first and chooses when to strike.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop, so it cannot reach f5 or g4, and does not guard d5 as a knight on f6 would. The knight does eye e5 and c5, so the cost is small, but it is a clumsy square for a developing move.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does little for the centre. The cost is small, so it is playable, but the rim is an unnatural square for a developing move and White takes space meanwhile.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5, where the knight would eye d4 and e3, but stands on the rim until it gets there and has cost a tempo. White develops and takes space in the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bd7.strategy: Cuts the queen off from d5, leaving the pawn undefended, and takes d7 from the b8-knight, while the bishop stands more passively than on f5 or g4. White develops and attacks d5 with c4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Be6.strategy: Blocks the e7-pawn, so neither …e6 nor …e5 can free the f8-bishop. The bishop guards d5, but 3.Ng5 attacks it and threatens Nxe6 fxe6 with doubled e-pawns, so Black loses time moving it again.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early and blocks the c8-bishop. 3.Ne5 attacks the queen at once and gains a tempo as it moves again.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to an exposed square. 3.Nc3 threatens Nb5, hitting the queen and c7, so Black loses time moving it again.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g5.name: Hungarian Opening: Wiedenhagen-Beta Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g5.strategy: Offers the g-pawn: 3.Nxg5 wins it, and …e5 or …h6 gain at most a tempo against the knight. The pawn is gone and the kingside is loosened for good.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 e5.name: King's Indian Attack: Omega-Delta Gambit
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 e5.strategy: Gives up the e-pawn: 3.Nxe5 wins it, and White can support the knight with d4 and keep the extra pawn without Black getting real compensation.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for no reason and walks into 3.Ne5+, which forces the king to move again. The king stays stuck in the centre while Black loses still more time.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.Bxh3 wins a whole piece, since nothing defends h3 and the rook on h8 is shut in behind the h7-pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares for ...Bxf3: the bishop can retake and land on the long diagonal, pointing at d5. White does not mind the exchange, which gives White the two bishops, and keeps developing in the same flexible way.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, before the bishop comes out. Black can exchange on f3 and White must recapture with the e-pawn, which doubles the f-pawns but gives White the two bishops and the open e-file; the exchange makes the order less accurate than developing first.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with the d-pawn at once. Black can still exchange on f3, and the recapture with the e-pawn doubles White's f-pawns for the two bishops and an open e-file, so White gives up the quiet fianchetto set-up for a more direct but less harmonious game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.Bg2 Nd7.name: King's Indian Attack: Keres Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.Bg2 Nd7.strategy: Develops the queenside knight, which supports e5 and f6 and prepares to back up the centre with the c-pawn. With the c8-bishop already outside the pawn chain, Black avoids the usual problem of a bishop shut in behind its pawns.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Backs up d5 with the c-pawn, a sturdy centre for a bishop that already stands outside the pawn chain. Black avoids the usual problem of the shut-in c8-bishop and keeps a flexible, solid set-up, at the price of a somewhat passive game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Bg4 3.Bg2 Bxf3.strategy: Gives up the bishop for the knight at once. White recaptures with the g2-bishop, which then eyes d5 and keeps the two bishops, so Black has spent time on an exchange that helps White's development and must keep an eye on the centre pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2.name: King's Indian Attack: Sicilian Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2.strategy: Develops the bishop on its long diagonal and prepares castling. White accepts that Black has taken space in the centre and does not fight for it at once; the plan is to undermine it later, with pieces and pawn breaks, from a safe king position.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges the d5 pawn at once with a flank pawn instead of holding back. The quiet set-up gives way to a fight for the centre, in which Black must either push on and gain space or exchange, while White aims for queenside pressure and an open position for the kingside bishop.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.d4.strategy: Puts a pawn in the centre at once and asks the c5 pawn what it intends. Black can gain space by pushing past or exchange and use the open c-file, and the bishop has not yet joined the game; sound and open, but it abandons the patient set-up that g3 was played for.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6.name: King's Indian Attack: French Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6.strategy: Adds a second guard to the d4 square, so White cannot easily plant a pawn there, and develops a piece while the e-pawn stays free to choose how to support d5. Black has the space in the centre and White the long diagonal.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, supporting d5 and watching e4, and leaves Black the choice between several set-ups for the other pieces. It is flexible but less direct than a knight move that fights for d4.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 g6.strategy: Gives Black a fianchetto of its own, so the bishop on g7 presses on the centre from a distance while the king finds a safe home. Solid and flexible, but slow: nothing is challenged yet, and Black waits to see where White puts the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4.name: Zukertort Opening: Reversed Grünfeld
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once: the pawn attacks c5, which nothing defends, while Black's pieces are still at home. White opens the game on good terms, and Black has to decide how to deal with the attacked pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles at once and keeps the set-up flexible, the way the system is usually played. The king is safe and the rook comes into play, but Black can claim more of the centre with a second central pawn, so White must prepare a break against it later instead of striking now.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d3.strategy: Builds a solid pawn base before castling, so that e4 can later be supported. It is slow: Black is free to occupy the centre, and White must then undermine it from a position that is short of space.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6.name: Zukertort Opening: Reversed Grünfeld
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, adding to the guard of d5 and watching e4, so the centre stays firm while White's d4 faces the c5-pawn. Black prefers development to defending c5 at once and accepts the tension.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 e6.strategy: Protects d5 and opens the f8-bishop's diagonal to c5, so the attacked pawn is guarded at once. A solid choice; the cost is the c8-bishop, which is shut in behind e6, and a slightly cramped position.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 cxd4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, giving up the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opening the c-file. White recaptures with the knight in the centre, where Black can challenge it, and the bishop already presses on d5; Black gets easy development in an open game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 e6 5.O-O.name: Zukertort Opening: Reversed Grünfeld
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 e6 5.O-O.strategy: Castles and leaves the central tension as it is: the king is safe behind the fianchettoed bishop and White's development is nearly complete. Black has to settle how to resolve the clash between d4 and c5.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 e6 5.dxc.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the central tension, and with it the d4 pawn that kept Black cramped. Black recaptures with the f8-bishop, which lands on an active diagonal, and the game becomes one of piece play with equal chances.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 e6 5.c3.strategy: Supports d4 with a pawn, so White can recapture there and keep a pawn in the centre. Solid, but it takes the c3 square from the knight and spends a tempo while the king is still uncastled, and Black gets time to develop freely.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6 5.O-.name: Zukertort Opening: Reversed Grünfeld
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6 5.O-.strategy: Castles and puts the king behind the fianchettoed bishop, leaving the tension between d4 and c5 untouched. White can now meet whatever Black does in the centre with the kingside development finished.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6 5.dx.strategy: Wins a pawn for the moment, but the pawn on c5 is hard to hold and White gives up the central pawn that restrained Black. Black regains it with natural development, so White has spent time to reach an equal and open game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nc6 4.d4 Nf6 5.c3.strategy: Backs up d4 with the c-pawn, so a pawn stays in the centre if Black exchanges there. A solid choice, but it costs a tempo and shuts the c-pawn in; Black develops freely and White has little to aim at beyond holding the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles at once, before deciding anything in the centre: the king is safe and the rook leaves the corner. White builds a solid position first and lets Black show where the centre stands.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: The patient route: the pawn takes a modest square and prepares to support e4, while the choice of where the queenside knight goes and when to castle stays open. Flexible and fully in the spirit of the system, but it lets Black decide the centre first.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre at once instead of building the slow system. Black can gain space on the queenside or exchange pawns and challenge White's central knight; either way White has left the quiet set-up and must play for central activity rather than a kingside attack.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6.strategy: Supports d5 with the e-pawn and opens the f8-bishop, a solid, flexible set-up in which pawns hold the centre. The cost is the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, so Black must find play for it while White chooses the plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece that adds to the pressure on d4 and prepares to take space with a second central pawn, as White does in the classical set-up. Natural and active; the cost is that Black commits the knight before knowing where White will put the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up with a fianchetto of Black's own: the bishop on g7 bears on the centre from a distance and the king gets a safe home. Sound but slow, since it does little against White's plan and leaves the centre to be settled later.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6 5.d3.name: King's Indian Attack: Sicilian Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6 5.d3.strategy: The move that defines the system: it supports a later e4 and keeps the centre solid, so White builds behind the pieces and aims for a space advantage and an attack on the kingside. It is patient and flexible rather than forcing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6 5.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once instead of preparing e4. If Black exchanges, White gets active pieces and a bishop bearing on d5, but Black holds the larger share of the central pawns; an open game that gives up the slow plan of the system.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c5 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6 5.b3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, so both bishops aim at the centre from the wings. Flexible and sound, but it spends a tempo on the queenside while Black can take more space in the centre, and White is left to find play with piece manoeuvres.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop aims along the long diagonal at d5 and the queenside, behind the f3 knight, and White is ready to castle. The centre stays open for now. Black's c6 makes d5 solid but takes the natural square from the b8 knight.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once and takes the game from the quiet kingside set-up into a fight for the centre, played with a wing pawn. If Black takes, White regains the pawn and the bishop on g2 gains scope as the centre opens. Black gets a solid, comfortable game in return.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.d3.strategy: Builds the chain that supports an e4 advance and frees the c1-bishop before the bishop develops. It reaches the same closed, manoeuvring game by a slower route, and the bishop on f1 does not yet press on d5, so Black can set up the centre in peace.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: The flexible developing move: it fights for e4, supports d5 and leaves the c8-bishop free to choose its square. Black keeps the solid c6 and d5 centre and develops with an eye on White's e4 plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before an ...e6 can shut it in, and hits the knight that guards d4 and e5. Black may trade the bishop for that knight whenever it likes, but then White gets the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bf5.strategy: Brings the bishop out before the knight and before ...e6 can shut it in, and it controls e4. The bishop is exposed there: Nh4 attacks it at once, and Black must move it, since Bg6 lets White take on g6 and gain the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O.strategy: Castles before any central decision: the king is safe, the rook leaves the corner and the fianchetto bishop is in place. White accepts that Black may swap the bishop for the f3 knight; the recapture keeps the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.d3.strategy: Goes straight for the standard set-up: the d-pawn supports an e4 advance and frees the c1-bishop, and castling follows next. It reaches the same positions as castling first, and Black can take on f3 whenever it likes, with the bishop recapturing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.h3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once. If it takes on f3, White recaptures with the bishop and has the bishop pair; if it retreats to h5, the g4 push becomes possible but weakens White's own kingside. The tempo spent on a rim pawn makes this playable rather than precise.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nd7.name: King's Indian Attack: Keres Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nd7.strategy: Develops the queen's knight on the natural square left by the c-pawn. It covers e5, where White's knight would like to go, and keeps f6 free for the other knight. Black builds a solid centre with the bishop outside the chain.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight to the square that covers e4 and d5, and keeps ...Nbd7 available for the other knight. Black reaches the usual set-up with the bishop outside the chain and a flexible order of development.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O e6.strategy: Supports d5 with a second pawn and opens the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop; with the light-squared bishop already outside, the pawn buries nothing. It is solid but slow: Black has developed only one minor piece, and the g4 bishop can still be challenged.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nd7 5.d.strategy: Gives up the slow d3 set-up for an immediate pawn centre that gains space and takes e5 away from Black. The f3 knight, which guards d4, is attacked by the g4-bishop, so White accepts the exchange and the bishop pair.

Chooses the slow, flexible set-up: the d-pawn supports an e4 advance and frees the c1-bishop while the b1 knight comes to d2. White accepts a bishop trade on f3, recapturing with the bishop, in return for a solid structure and kingside pressure. The game stays closed and manoeuvring.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nd7 5.h.strategy: Asks the g4-bishop to decide at once. After a trade on f3 White has the bishop pair; after a retreat to h5 the bishop stays active and White must weigh weakening its own king with g4. The tempo on a rim pawn means White's development lags, so it is playable rather than precise.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Bg4 4.O-O Nd7 5.d.strategy: Completes the knight development and puts a piece on a square that controls e4 and d5. Black now has a compact set-up: the c6 and d5 pawns hold the centre, the bishop sits outside them, and White must find a way to make progress.

Builds a second pawn behind d5 and frees the dark-squared bishop, the light-squared bishop being already outside the chain. Black gives up the idea of ...e5, which White's d4 pawn controls, and plays for a compact, solid structure.

Trades the bishop for the knight at once instead of waiting. Black removes the defender of White's centre and keeps a solid structure, but hands over the bishop pair without a gain in return, and the recapturing bishop eyes d5 from f3.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O.strategy: Gets the king to safety and the rook off the corner before any central decision. White keeps every option for the pawn centre, and the bishop already aims at Black's queenside along the long diagonal, behind the f3 knight.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, so the fight for the centre is played with a wing pawn instead of d3 and e4. The bishop on g2 gains power on the long diagonal as the centre opens, and White accepts that Black gets an easy, solid game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Sets up the pawn chain first, to support e4 and free the c1-bishop, and leaves castling for a move. It reaches the same positions as castling first once Black has chosen a square for the c8-bishop, so the choice of move order costs White nothing.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bg4.name: King's Indian Attack: Yugoslav Variation
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop on the diagonal that attacks the f3 knight, before an ...e6 can close it in. The knight guards d4 and e5, so Black pressures it at once. The bishop can trade itself for the knight, which gives White the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5.name: King's Indian Attack, with Bf5
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain on the other diagonal, where it controls e4 and so hinders White's natural e-pawn advance. The price is that the bishop on f5 can be harassed and Black has to watch its retreat.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O e6.strategy: Closes the c8-bishop in behind the pawn chain before it has found a square, in exchange for solidity: d5 gets a second pawn and the dark-squared bishop is freed. The price is a passive light-squared bishop, which is why Black usually places it outside the chain first.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Blocks the bishop's diagonal on d3, where the pawn is guarded several times, and controls e4 so the bishop loses its hold there. White keeps a solid structure, frees the c1-bishop and prepares to bring out the b1 knight.

Takes space in the centre at once and keeps the structure solid, but gives Black a free hand: the bishop on f5 is well placed outside the chain, and Black completes development without difficulty. A calm, level game with little for White to press.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.N.strategy: Attacks the f5 bishop at once. The knight stands on the rim with few useful squares, and the bishop usually keeps its good diagonal with ...Bg6 or ...Bg4, so White gains little for the time spent unless Black trades on g6 and hands over the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Reinforces d5 with a second pawn and opens the way for the dark-squared bishop. With the light-squared bishop already outside the chain, the e6 pawn buries no piece, and Black gets a solid, compact set-up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.name: King's Indian Attack, with Bf5
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's pieces and gives the bishop a retreat on h7 if White harasses it. It costs a tempo on the kingside while White goes on developing, but the bishop keeps its active diagonal.

Develops the last minor piece while keeping ...e6 and ...h6 for later. It leaves the f5 bishop without a prepared retreat, so Nh4 attacks it at once and Black must move it, since Bg6 lets White take on g6 and gain the bishop pair.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.name: King's Indian Attack, with Bf5
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Develops the last minor piece to the square that supports e4 and keeps the c-pawn free to move. White now has everything ready to challenge Black's centre with either pawn, and keeps the position flexible.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.name: King's Indian Attack, with Bf5
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Hits the bishop at once: Black must retreat it or trade it for the knight, which hands White the bishop pair. But the knight stands on the rim with few good squares, and the central development waits; an ambitious idea the simple development does not need.

Strikes at d5 at once: the exchange of the c-pawn for Black's centre pawn gives White a share of the centre with the bishop on g2 behind it. White swaps the slow e4 plan for a more open fight, and Black, with its bishop outside the chain, has a comfortable, solid game.

Strikes at d5 now that Black's ...h6 has spent a tempo, forcing Black to settle the central tension before White has played e4. White gives up the slow plan for a more open fight, with the fianchetto bishop on the long diagonal behind it.

Develops the last minor piece to the square that supports e4 and keeps the c-pawn free to move, so the central play is not hurried. White ignores the h6 pawn and goes on with development; Black's tempo has bought the bishop a retreat and nothing else.
Attacks the f5 bishop, but the h6 pawn gives it h7 as a retreat, so the attack loses its sting. The knight on the rim has few useful squares and White's development waits.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.name: Réti Opening: Anglo-Slav Variation, with g3
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Keeps the centre closed and holds d5 with a second pawn instead of releasing the tension. The bishop stays outside the chain and the dark-squared bishop is freed; Black accepts that White may take on d5 and change the pawn structure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.name: King's Indian Attack, with Bf5
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bf5 5.d.strategy: Resolves the tension by taking the pawn. White regains it and the d-file opens, so the queens can come off. Black trades its centre pawn for White's c-pawn and gets a calm, nearly symmetrical game, with the bishop well placed outside the chain.

Develops the last minor piece and leaves the tension in the centre where it is. If White exchanges on d5 and brings the queen to b3, it hits both d5 and b7, so Black has to answer accurately; the move is playable but less clear than holding d5 with a pawn.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bg4 5.d.strategy: Abandons the slow d3 and e4 set-up for an immediate pawn on d4, which gains space and takes e5 away from Black. The f3 knight, which guards d4, is attacked by the g4-bishop, so White is ready for the exchange and the bishop pair.

Chooses the King's Indian Attack set-up: the d-pawn supports an e4 advance and frees the c1-bishop while the b1 knight comes to d2. White accepts a bishop trade on f3, recapturing with the bishop to keep the pair, and plays a closed, manoeuvring game with kingside play as the plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2 Nf6 4.O-O Bg4 5.h.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide at once. After a trade on f3 White has the bishop pair; after a retreat to h5 the bishop stays active and White must weigh weakening its own king with g4. The tempo spent on a rim pawn makes this playable rather than precise.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2.strategy: Fianchettoes the bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at d5 and the queenside behind the f3 knight. Black has mirrored the idea with ...g6, so both sides develop slowly and the fight for the centre is postponed.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre at once and keeps Black's d5 pawn where it is, with the bishop to follow on g2. The pawn on d4 gives White space and a clear plan, but it is soon attacked by the g7-bishop, so the knight has to keep guarding it.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 before the bishop is out. If Black takes on c4, White can win the pawn back with a queen check, but only by bringing the queen out early; if Black holds d5, White has committed the c-pawn before choosing a set-up. Playable, but less flexible than developing first.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Completes the mirror set-up: the bishop aims along the long diagonal at b2, and Black's king gets the usual fianchetto shelter. Black keeps the pawn moves flexible and decides the centre only once White shows its plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it backs d5 and watches e4, and keeps the fianchetto of the bishop for the next move. A solid, flexible order: Black builds the mirror set-up and sees whether White commits in the centre.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 c6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn, so no piece has to guard it, and leaves the c8-bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain. Solid but modest: Black spends a move on structure before the kingside is ready and gives White time to arrange the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O.strategy: Castles to bring the king to safety and the rook towards the centre, while the fianchetto bishop stays on its long diagonal. White decides against rushing the centre; where the pawns go next shapes the whole game.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre at once. The pawn on d4 is attacked by the g7-bishop and guarded by the knight and the queen, so Black can challenge it immediately. White gains space and a clear plan, at the cost of the flexible waiting set-up.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d3.strategy: Controls e4, opens the c1-bishop and keeps castling for later. A slower, flexible set-up that decides the centre only once Black shows its plan, and one that reaches the same structures as the main line by another route.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5.strategy: Takes the centre with a second pawn, backed by the g7-bishop, and keeps White's pieces off d4 and f4. The price is that the bishop is now blocked by its own pawn, so Black must be ready to open the position to bring it to life.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight backs d5, watches e4 and prepares castling, completing a mirror set-up without committing a pawn. Black decides the centre later, and White, already castled, has to show its own plan first.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O c6.strategy: Backs d5 with a pawn and lets the c8-bishop develop outside the pawn chain. Solid, but it spends a move on the pawn before the knights are out and lets White build up in the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5 5.d3.strategy: Meets the broad Black centre by keeping the structure solid instead of attacking it: the d3 pawn controls e4, frees the c1-bishop and prepares to bring out the queen's knight. White aims for a slow game in which Black's pawn duo has to prove itself.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5 5.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once instead of waiting. If Black takes, White regains the pawn with a queen check; if Black pushes ...d4, the game closes and both sides play on the wings. But ...e4 gains a tempo on the f3 knight, so it is less comfortable than the quiet main plan.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5 5.d4.strategy: Hits e5 at once, but ...e4 answers with tempo: the pawn attacks the f3 knight and takes space, and the g7-bishop eyes any knight that settles on e5. White ends up in a closed centre where Black has the extra room.

1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5 5.d3.name: King's Indian Attack: Pachman System
1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.O-O e5 5.d3.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it adds a defender to d5, without blocking the g7-bishop's diagonal or the f-pawn. Both central pawns are backed, and Black is close to castling with a flexible, solid set-up.
Blocks the g7-bishop's diagonal, so e5 loses its only defender and Nxe5 wins a pawn. Black castles and develops with some play, but a clean pawn down is more than that lead in development is worth.

Answers the question of how to keep e5 safe: a second defender lets Black go on developing while the g7-bishop keeps its diagonal. It commits to the d5-e5 pawn pair with the knight in front of the c-pawn, so pieces rather than ...c6 hold d5. A slow fight over the centre follows.
